result: The synthesized core-shell MNPs heat efficiently in AMF while horse ferritin does not, demonstrating that the synthesized particles are superior transducers for magnetothermal stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 provide theoretical calculations and experimental measurements showing that horse ferritin has negligible dipole interaction energy and heating capacity compared to the synthesized core-shell MNPs. The data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 supports these quantitative comparisons, establishing the superiority of the synthesized particles.

result: The authors synthesized optimized core-shell MNPs with specific dimensions and heating properties suitable for magnetothermal stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C34-C37 and C103 describe the synthesis and characterization of Co-Mn ferrite core-shell MNPs with specific dimensions (8.0±1.0 nm core, 2.25 nm shell, 5.4±1.4 nm PMA coating) and high SLP (733.3±2.8 W/g). These are well-documented experimental measurements supported by TEM data in Figure 1D.

result: Membrane-bound MNPs produce localized, rapid heating and cooling at the cell membrane without bulk tissue heating, unlike MNP suspensions which heat the entire bath slowly.
evaluation: Claims C38-C45 describe temperature measurements using DyLight 550 fluorescence showing that membrane-bound MNPs heat locally (several degrees at membrane) with fast cooling (seconds), while suspensions heat the entire bath (2°C) with slow cooling (>1 min). Data in Figure 2C-F support these kinetic differences, and the calculated heating power per MNP (2.55±0.94 fW) matches theoretical predictions.

result: TRPV1 expression renders hippocampal neurons heat-sensitive, with firing rates increasing dramatically at 37-39°C, while maintaining normal neuronal function at physiological temperatures.
evaluation: Claims C46-C51 demonstrate that TRPV1+ neurons show temperature-independent firing from 32-36°C but increased firing from 1.5±1.2 to 13±3 APs per 5s when heated from 37-39°C, while control neurons show slight decreases. The data in Figure 3A and supporting analysis of calcium transient shapes confirm TRPV1 sensitization without disrupting normal function.

result: AMF application to MNP-decorated TRPV1+ neurons produces rapid, reproducible neuronal activation with latencies of 2-3 seconds and 2°C membrane heating.
evaluation: Claims C52-C56 and C104-C107 provide quantitative data showing significant increases in spiking frequency during and after AMF (p=0.0028 and p=0.0002), with 87% of neurons firing within 5s and 64% within 2-3s. The Poisson-fitted latency distribution (λ=2.18±0.17s) and 2°C membrane heating (C104) are well-documented. The 87.5% reproducibility (C105) demonstrates reliability. These represent the fastest magnetothermal stimulation reported.

result: Magnetothermal genetic stimulation using AMF-heated membrane-bound MNPs and TRPV1 expression provides tetherless deep brain activation sufficient to evoke specific motor behaviors in awake mice across three brain regions.
evaluation: Claims C1-C4 and C29-C32 describe the main finding: successful behavioral activation in three brain regions (motor cortex, dorsal striatum, ridge between dorsal/ventral striatum) producing behaviors consistent with prior optogenetic/chemogenetic studies. The experimental data throughout the manuscript, including behavioral tracking and controls, support this central claim.

result: Motor cortex stimulation evoked running behavior in all tested mice with significant increases in linear and angular speed, tight temporal correlation with AMF application, and requirement for both TRPV1 and membrane-targeted MNPs.
evaluation: Claims C60-C69 provide comprehensive behavioral data showing all 6 mice (14 trials) exhibited running with 16-fold increase in linear speed (p=5.9×10⁻⁶) and 8-fold increase in angular speed (p=5.2×10⁻⁹). Response latency (22.8±2.6s) and offset (14.7±2.5s) are documented. Critical controls (C66-C69) demonstrate necessity of both TRPV1 and membrane-targeted MNPs (p=1.1×10⁻⁵), with proper antibody targeting essential.

result: Striatum stimulation evoked unilateral rotation around the body axis with small turn radii, consistent with prior chemogenetic studies.
evaluation: Claims C71-C75 describe rotational behavior (22±5 mm radius circles at 19.3±2.2 mm/s, 4.7±0.8 rev/min) in 4 mice across 12 trials, with 6-fold increase in angular speed (p=3.4×10⁻⁷). The contralateral turning in 11/12 trials and consistency with prior capsaicin-TRPV1 activation studies (C75) validate the specificity of the response.

result: Deep striatum stimulation at the ridge between dorsal and ventral striatum caused freezing-of-gait with near-complete immobilization of limbs while preserving head movement.
evaluation: Claims C77, C79-C80 describe FOG behavior with linear speed decreasing from 17.7±2.2 mm/s to 1.04±0.13 mm/s (p=0.0006), indistinguishable from a fixed marker (0.52±0.11 mm/s). The specific phenotype (limb immobilization with preserved head movement) is documented in Figure 6D and videos, demonstrating precise spatial targeting.

result: Magnetothermal stimulation provides temporal precision with behavior onset within 15-20s and offset within 15s of AMF application, allowing multiple stimulations within experimental sessions.
evaluation: Claims C7 and C81-C85 document tight temporal correlation between AMF and behavior. The 15-20s latency (C81) is explained by weaker in vivo field strength (C82-C83), with heating rate proportional to field strength squared. Fast offset (15s, C84) and ability to perform 3-4 one-minute stimulations in 10-15 min (C85) demonstrate temporal control.

result: Membrane targeting of MNPs using antibodies provides spatial specificity, cell-type selectivity, and requires 200-fold less nanoparticle material than suspension-based approaches.
evaluation: Claims C33 and C86-C91 describe the membrane targeting strategy using A2B5 antibody (highest density, fastest heating) and alternatives (anti-CD56, anti-CD90, anti-GFP). Histological data (Figure 5—figure supplements 5-6) show limited MNP diffusion and cell-specific binding. The 200-fold reduction in MNP amount (500 ng vs. prior suspension methods) is a significant practical improvement.

result: Magnetothermal stimulation is repeatable over multiple days without observable damage, with histology showing intact MNP-decorated neurons after 20 stimulations.
evaluation: Claims C92-C93 demonstrate safety and repeatability: 7-8 trials over several days without behavioral changes, and histology after 20 one-minute AMF applications showing intact neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 7). This addresses a key concern about potential thermal damage.

result: The approach provides genetically targetable, spatially precise, repeatable, and temporally controlled activation without permanent implants, using localized membrane heating.
evaluation: Claims C8, C27-C28, and C112 summarize the key advantages: genetic targeting (viral TRPV1 delivery), spatial precision (antibody-directed MNP binding), repeatability (demonstrated experimentally), temporal control (fast on/off kinetics from localized heating), and no permanent implants. These claims are supported by the collective experimental evidence throughout the manuscript.

result: Both AAV5 and lentivirus vectors successfully delivered TRPV1 to enable robust behavioral stimulation in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C59 and C110 describe the viral delivery approach. While C59 correctly notes that robust stimulation requires TRPV1 overexpression (necessitating viral delivery), C110 confirms both viral systems worked successfully. The experimental data showing successful behavioral responses validate this approach.

result: The tetherless nature of magnetothermal stimulation enables novel experimental paradigms including selective stimulation in group settings and spatially-controlled activation.
evaluation: Claims C16, C94-C95 describe potential future applications (social behavioral assays, selective group stimulation, field geometry control) but are speculative. While the tetherless nature is demonstrated, these specific applications have not been experimentally validated in the manuscript.

result: The technique is scalable to larger brains including non-human primates and humans, with advantages over optogenetics for multiple-site stimulation and avoiding displacement issues.
evaluation: Claims C96-C101 discuss scalability and advantages for primate applications. While C96 documents the current setup (7.5 kW, 300 cm³) and C97 notes larger power sources exist, the actual application to primates is speculative. The theoretical advantages (C98-C101) regarding brain movement and multi-site stimulation are logical but undemonstrated.

result: Future non-invasive MNP delivery via bloodstream may be possible using focused ultrasound to transiently open the blood-brain barrier.
evaluation: Claim C102 cites prior work showing focused ultrasound can make the blood-brain barrier permeable to virus particles. While the citation supports this possibility, the actual application to MNP delivery for magnetothermal stimulation is speculative and not demonstrated in this work.

result: The manuscript correctly contextualizes magnetothermal stimulation relative to existing techniques (optogenetics, DREADDs) and established principles of magnetic field interactions and superparamagnetic particles.
evaluation: Claims C9-C20 provide background on existing techniques and magnetic principles. These are well-supported by appropriate citations and represent accurate characterizations of: optogenetics limitations (C9-C13), DREADDs kinetics (C14), magnetic field properties (C15), and superparamagnetic particle physics (C18-C20). The citations to prior work are appropriate.

result: The observed behavioral responses are consistent with prior optogenetic and chemogenetic studies in the same brain regions.
evaluation: Claims C31, C70, C75-C76, C78, C109, and C111 compare the observed behaviors to prior studies. The citations are appropriate and the behavioral phenotypes (motor cortex running, striatum rotation, deep striatum FOG) match those reported in prior optogenetic/chemogenetic work, validating the specificity of the magnetothermal approach.
